To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the communication complexity of any perfectly secure protocol is Ω(gn) for circuits with g gates, and that the communication complexity is O(g2n) for any circuit.
the communication complexity of any perfect maliciously secure protocol implementing a circuit C of size g is Ω(ng) and that the communication complexity is at most O(nlg2g).
the communication complexity of perfectly secure multiparty computation is Ω(nlgg) in the standard model, where g is the number of gates of the circuit, and that this is tight up to a constant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
showing a tight lower bound for perfect maliciously secure MPC. We believe that our techniques are of independent interest and may be used for proving lower bounds in other cryptographic settings.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the communication complexity of perfectly secure MPC in the standard model is Θ(ng) bits.
the optimal communication complexity for perfectly malicious secure MPC in the standard model is Ω(g) bits for circuits with g gates.
for n = 3 t + 1, any circuit of size g, and any field size l, the communication complexity of perfectly secure MPC is Θ(ng/l).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the communication complexity for perfect maliciously secure MPC is Θ(ng).
the optimal communication complexity of perfect MPC is Θ(ng) bits, where n and g are the number of parties and the size of the circuit, respectively.
perfect maliciously secure MPC is essentially as communication expensive as the corresponding semi-honest setting, up to a constant.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in contrast to semi-honest security, there is a significant communication complexity cost to achieving perfect malicious security.
, in the perfect setting, the cost of malicious security in the standard model is essentially the cost of evaluating the circuit itself.
, despite being a very strong notion, perfect maliciously secure computation does not incur any asymptotically worse overhead than semi-honest secure computation.
